newsitem.title: ITALY: No change yet on budget boycott - Italy opposition.
newsitem.headline: No change yet on budget boycott - Italy opposition.

text.p: Italy's main opposition said on Wednesday that the government had not yet made enough concessions over its tough 1997 budget and that it would not take part in a vote on the package in the Senate (upper house).

"For now, representatives will remain in the Senate, we will present our amendments but we won't take part in the vote on a budget we think will ruin the country," Silvio Berlusconi, leader of the centre-right Freedom Alliance, said.

Prime Minister Romano Prodi's 1997 budget bill, designed to slash 62.5 trillion lire ($40.7 billion) off next year's deficit, is due to be debated in the Senate on December 10 and to return to the lower Chamber of Deputies on December 16.
The Freedom Alliance refused to take part last month in sessions of the Chamber which approved the austerity package.
The boycott began over plans by the centre-left government to seek special powers that will allow the cabinet to legislate on some areas of fiscal policy without recourse to parliament.
Parties in the ruling "Olive Tree" coalition offered what they said were concessions to the opposition on Tuesday night to try to ensure the opposition takes part in voting.
The concessions include a proposal to set up a commission of both houses of parliament to monitor the cabinet's use of any special powers on fiscal policy.
Berlusconi said the centre-right's opposition remained firm. "It is not possible to attribute full powers to the government on fiscal policy," he told a news conference.
Gianfranco Fini, leader of the far-right National Alliance, said the centre-right could vote in the Senate only if such powers on a planned new regional tax (IREP) were withdrawn.
"If not, we remain in the same situation as in the Chamber," he said.

The opposition's lower house boycott followed a huge Freedom Alliance demonstration in Rome to protest against the budget, which is designed to help Italy make the grade for Europe's planned single currency.
